item.title: Three dead and several injured in shooting at food festival near Seattle's Space Needle
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c78gjyx4q2yo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Three dead and several injured in shooting at food festival near Seattle's Space Needle - Published Three people have been killed and several others injured following a shooting at a food festival near the Space Needle in Seattle on Sunday, the city fire department said. Mayor Katie Wilson said one suspect was taken into custody following the incident at the Seattle Centre, which had been hosting the annual Bite of Seattle food festival across the weekend when the shots were fired at around 18:00 local time. A second suspect fled the scene and is yet to be apprehended, assistant chief of Seattle Police Tyrone Davis added. He said it is believed the suspects were shooting at each other. Two deaths were confirmed at the scene, with one person dying later in hospital. Those injured include a two-year-old boy, officials said. Videos shared online showed people taking shelter inside the city's iconic Space Needle. People could be seen crouched on the ground, taking cover behind pillars and shelves of merchandise in the Space Needle's lobby during the shooting. The Seattle Police Department said an investigation remains ongoing and urged the public to avoid the area. Wilson said in a statement that she wanted to "thank the Seattle police officers who responded to the scene and took a suspect into custody". She had originally announced two suspects had been taken into custody before updating her statement later on Sunday evening. Four of the injured were taken to hospital in a stable condition, while a fifth chose not to, the fire department said. Representatives for Seattle and Washington state have condemned the shooting as an act of "senseless violence". "My prayers are with the families of the victims, and the responders as they work to keep people safe," Washington Governor Bob Ferguson said on social media. Congresswoman Pramila Jayapal, who represents Seattle, added: "Our hearts go out to all those impacted by this senseless violence," she wrote on social media. "We are in close touch with Seattle Mayor Katie Wilson and Governor Bob Ferguson, and co-ordinating across multiple levels of government to get updates on the situation." Wilson also condemned the shooting as an "act of horrific violence". "Impacted families are living through the worst moment of their lives, and an entire community is trying to understand how a gathering built around culture, connection, and joy ended in gunfire." "Tonight, our attention belongs to the people whose lives were taken, those fighting to recover, and the families beside them," she added. "Seattle grieves with you, and we will stand with you in the difficult days ahead." Related topics - Published1 day ago

item.title: Berlin Pride attack suspect shot and killed during police operation
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c62eg899l99o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Berlin Pride attack suspect shot and killed during police operation - Published The man suspected of carrying out what authorities say was likely an "Islamist terror attack" at Berlin Pride has been shot and killed by police. Officers opened fire when Abdul Ballout, a 21-year-old German citizen with Lebanese heritage, rushed at them with a knife in Spandau, a western borough of Berlin. It brought an end to a massive manhunt that was launched after a white van was driven into a crowd of people near Tiergarten park just before 22:00 (local time) on Saturday evening, killing one woman and injuring at least 29 others. Police say following the ramming, several people were injured in a stabbing attack. Speaking to reporters on Sunday, German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt said evidence pointed to it being an "Islamist terror attack". "We are dealing with a suspected perpetrator, who had previously drawn attention to himself through a high volume of criminal offences, radicalisation and affiliation with the Islamist scene," Dobrindt said. A statement released by the Berlin public prosecutor's office revealed further details about Ballout's criminal history. In May 2025, prosecutors said he travelled via Turkey to Lebanon, with the intention of joining the Islamic State group (IS) in Syria. While in Lebanon he allegedly made contact with several individuals he believed were members of IS. He was arrested in Lebanon in July 2025 and sentenced to three months in prison for incitement to religious and sectarian conflict. Then in November 2025 he returned to Germany where he was arrested at Berlin Brandenburg Airport and held in pre-trial detention. In May this year, he was sentenced to one year and 10 months in prison for "preparing a serious act of violence endangering the state". The decision was deferred for six months and he was placed under the supervision of a parole officer. He was previously convicted of assault and robbery in 2022, and of robbing a victim of headphones in 2020. Dobrindt said Germany's threat level would be raised following the attack, while other states were also being briefed about the attack and advised to review their security measures for major events. On Sunday, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz visited the scene of the attack in Tiergarten park. He later spoke outside a church service that paid tribute to victims, where he pledged to "defend the freedom and openness of our lives". "These extremists have no place in our society," he said, adding that Germany would not allow the "poison of terrorism" to affect its society. Berlin police have said people were hit on Ahornsteig street, which is a long path stretching across the Tiergarten park, largely in a forested area. Meanwhile, German media say those injured in the attack are no longer in a life-threatening condition. Saturday's attack shattered the joy and revelry of Berlin's Christopher Street Day, where hundreds of thousands spill onto the city streets for one of Europe's most famous Pride events. Christopher Street Day commemorates the first known uprising among the LGBT community in New York City in 1969 at the Stonewall Inn, which is located on Christopher Street. A clean-up event due to take place at Tiergarten park and a breakfast market scheduled for Sunday morning were both cancelled following the attack. Later in the day, some members of the LGBT community returned to the iconic Brandenburg Gate for an impromptu vigil. Speakers condemned extremism in all its manifestations, but they also criticised the government for a lack of support, singling out recent budget cuts for queer organisations. Armin Duenhoelter from Wolfsburg, who works as a drag artist, was backstage at the main stage when the attack happened. He told Agency France-Presse that he was still shocked but vowed to be back for next year's pride celebration. "We won't let it beat us down," he said. Get in touch Did you attend Berlin Pride? If it is safe to do so, get in touch. - Published13 hours ago

item.title: Netanyahu accuses NYC Mayor Mamdani of 'fomenting hate' after arrest threat
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c5yegvd9ddeo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Netanyahu accuses NYC Mayor Mamdani of 'fomenting hate' after arrest threat - Published Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said he planned to attend the UN General Assembly in New York City this autumn, despite the city's mayor, Zohran Mamdani, making threats to arrest him. Mamdani walked back that threat last week, acknowledging he lacked the legal power to arrest Netanyahu on a warrant issued by the International Criminal Court, the world's top war-crimes court. The Israeli leader told Fox News on Sunday that he was "not concerned" about Mamdani's previous pledge and accused the mayor of "fomenting hate". "He's supposed to be the mayor of all New Yorkers, Jews, Christians, Muslims, everyone, but he's trying to turn one group against the other," Netanyahu said. Netanyahu referenced a pair of stabbings in New York on Thursday, in which a suspect stabbed a Jewish man and an Asian man just blocks apart. The suspect allegedly shouted the phrase "Allahu akbar" while committing the stabbings, according to police. He has been charged with hate crimes relating to each victim. Both men survived the attacks, which drew condemnations from the city's Jewish and Asian American leaders. In the aftermath, Netanyahu said Jewish New Yorkers were "afraid right now." The mayor's office did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Mamdani, a staunch supporter of Palestinian rights, made his opposition to the Israeli military operation in Gaza a central plank of his campaign last year. In an address last week, he called Netanyahu a "war criminal." As part of that platform while campaigning, Mamdani promised to enforce a 2024 arrest warrant for Netanyahu from the International Criminal Court (ICC), which accused the prime minister of committing war crimes in Gaza. Israel has denied charges that it has committed war crimes in Gaza, and Netanyahu called the charges "bogus". The Israeli military entered Gaza after the Hamas-led attack in Israel on 7 October 2023. About 1,200 people were killed and 251 were taken hostage. Over 73,000 people have been killed in Israeli attacks in Gaza since then, including more than 21,000 children, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN. Last week, after the New York Times pressed Mamdani on his pledge to arrest Netanyahu, Mamdani said his administration had reviewed the law and found: "We do not have the independent legal authority to enforce this warrant". Mamdani urged the federal government to arrest the prime minister, and said: "Benjamin Netanyahu is not welcome in New York City." - Published4 days ago

item.title: UK PM pledges continued support for Ukraine ahead of Zelensky visit
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cy8me5vyjg2o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
PM pledges continued support for Ukraine ahead of Zelensky visit - Published Andy Burnham has pledged to continue the UK's "unwavering" support for Ukraine ahead of meeting Volodymyr Zelensky on Monday. The Ukrainian president will become the prime minister's first international visitor since he took office a week ago, which No 10 said "illustrates the strength of the relationship between the two nations". They will visit a naval base, where Burnham will announce the sharing of the intellectual property behind the UK's new "Stone Cloak" electronic warfare system, enabling Ukraine to produce the technology at scale. Burnham told the BBC's Laura Kuenssberg ahead of the visit that he was looking forward to it and that his support for Ukraine was "unwavering - it is 100%". The Stone Cloak jammers are the size of a tablet computer and are designed to block the detection of any drones they are fitted to. The Ministry of Defence has already given thousands of the devices to Ukrainian forces to bolster their drone operations. Downing Street said that following its deployment in Ukraine, the technology will be built into the UK's next generation of long-range weapons. It said this would include Project Brakestop, a government programme to develop low-cost cruise missiles - self-propelled guided weapons that fly like normal aircraft for much of their flight. Burnham said in a statement on Sunday evening: "Stone Cloak is the best of homegrown British innovation and proven on the frontline, and it will be vital to protecting our security in both our countries." During Monday's visit, the two leaders will also meet more than 200 Ukrainian military personnel who have spent the last three weeks taking part in a maritime exercise in the UK. Exercise Sea Breeze is aimed at strengthening warfighting capabilities and counter-mine measures in the Black Sea. Britain's backing of Ukraine has been constant since Russia's invasion four years ago, and the UK has committed £25bn in funding, external for the country's warfighting efforts. In one of his first calls after becoming prime minister last Monday, Burnham spoke to Zelensky and invited him to visit the UK "at the earliest opportunity". Zelensky wrote on X shortly afterwards: "I truly appreciate that the support for Ukraine and our people will remain steadfast." Burnham's predecessor, Sir Keir Starmer, visited Kyiv on his final full day as Labour leader. During that trip, he announced fresh funding worth £255m (€300m) for Ukraine's fight against Russia and was awarded Ukraine's Order of Freedom. Asked if he was concerned about changes of leadership in Britain, and in France next year, Zelensky said: "Of course I'm afraid of changes, of course we are afraid because we are in the war each day. "But again the priority is the relation between nations, not just between just people. I'm sure that these relations will not change, or we have to do our best not to lose such very good relations." He added: "I hope we will never lose strong relations with the UK during or after the war." Sir Keir replied: "You won't." Burnham told the BBC in his first major interview since becoming prime minister: "My support for Ukraine is unwavering - it is 100%. And I will do what, in Ukraine, people think is the right thing that they need." He also paid tribute to Sir Keir's "huge personal support" for Zelensky, adding: "He will get exactly the same from me." - Ten killed in Russian attack on drone exhibition near Kyiv - Published2 days ago

item.title: Israeli settlers set fire to mosques, cars and farm land in West Bank, Palestinians say
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cjrv77gl4deo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Israeli settlers set fire to mosques, cars and farm land in West Bank, Palestinians say - Published Israeli settlers have set fire to two mosques, as well as cars and agricultural land in the occupied West Bank, Palestinian officials say, as tensions in the territory continue to flare. The latest attacks come two days after a clash between settlers and Palestinians near the village of Tal, which left four Palestinians and two Israelis dead. Both sides accused the other of provoking the violence. The confrontation has further inflamed the situation in the West Bank, which has seen ever growing violence by extremist settlers against Palestinians, encouraged by far-right elements in the current Israeli government. Palestinian reports say that two villages in the occupied West Bank came under attack from settlers overnight, with cars vandalised, property stolen and hate graffiti spray painted on walls. The mayor of Qusra said that settlers set fire to a mosque that was under construction. Abdul Azim Wadi said that settlers spray painted graffiti that included the word "revenge" on the walls of the mosque. The Israeli military has said that troops were sent to Qusra and that police would investigate and collect evidence. Palestinian officials say that in a separate incident, settlers set fire to another mosque in the village of Kour and sprayed slogans on its walls. Since the deadly clash on Friday in Tal, Palestinians say that there have been multiple settler attacks on villages across the West Bank. The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) has carried out raids and arrested more than 130 individuals over the weekend in what it has called a "counter-terrorism" operation. The Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu responded to the incident in Tal by vowing to take "powerful action". That includes the possible demolition of the homes of two of the Palestinians who were allegedly involved. The Palestinian village of Sarra sits next to Tal, with the outpost of Havat Gilad clearly visible on the hill next door. Hanan Turabi speaks to the BBC in tears beside her house - one of six buildings torched by settlers that day, residents said, with more than a dozen others attacked with stones. Neighbours swept waves of blackened water and ash from the house, as sooty furniture was loaded onto a truck outside. Hanan described seeing crowds of settlers running towards her across the hillside. She said she stayed in her house until the last second before fleeing with four children. "They came from everywhere," she said. "We tried to escape but they followed us and threw stones." She said she wanted to stay and protect her home but had to choose between her house burning or her family. Kaied Ahmad Turabi, from Miami, was visiting his parents and sister in the village when the attack happened. He was filmed fighting with settlers on a neighbour's porch. He was just out of hospital when he spoke to the BBC. He had a large black eye, several cuts and bruises, and a wound on his head that he said had needed 12 stitches. "I worked all my life with Jewish people, but these people... they all had covered faces, all of them had a lot of stuff – sticks, and things in their pockets. They came ready," he said. Hours later, we were with residents watching the back entrance to the village when settlers were spotted on its outskirts again. We watched dozens of young men stream up the road, answering a call to barricade and defend the village. Israeli soldiers stood guard to separate the groups, as the settlers slowly melted away. For the Palestinians, it was a different method of crowd control - tear gas fired repeatedly to push them back down the road. Some young men ran through clouds of gas to try and bury the cannisters with soil, or kick them away to chants of "Palestine, Palestine", as the soldiers steadily advanced. Israel's military said on Sunday it was working to prevent "incidents of nationalist crime" - its term for attacks by extremist Israeli settlers there. But while Israeli leaders publicly condemn extremist violence, they have overseen a rapid growth in the wildcat settlement outposts that human rights groups say are fuelling attacks on Palestinians. Israel's prime minister said he would speed up the establishment and legalisation of farm outposts in the West Bank, in response to the killing of Israelis in Tal on Friday. New Israeli outposts have already appeared in the area since then - one near Sarra is visible from the main road. There has been a sharp increase in settler attacks in the West Bank in recent months. It has drawn international condemnation, but shown little or no sign of being reversed. The situation had already deteriorated before the Hamas-led attacks on Israel on October 7, 2023. But since the subsequent war waged by Israel against Hamas in Gaza erupted, settler violence in the West Bank has escalated. The UN says 1,114 Palestinians have been killed in the West Bank, the vast majority by the IDF. It says at least 35 of the deaths have involved attacks by settlers. It says 41 Israelis, including civilians and security personnel, have been killed in Palestinian attacks or during Israeli military operations in the West Bank since the start of the Gaza war. Israel has built hundreds of settlements housing 700,000 Jews since it occupied the West Bank and East Jerusalem - land Palestinians want, along with Gaza, for a hoped-for future state - during the 1967 Middle East war. An estimated 3.3 million Palestinians live alongside them. The settlements are illegal under international law. - Published2 days ago

item.title: Millions see leaked copy of The Odyssey movie on X
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c1m1ev5j3m2o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Millions see leaked copy of The Odyssey movie on X - Published Director Christopher Nolan wants people to watch The Odyssey on the biggest screen possible - but two million people reportedly viewed a social media post containing a leaked copy of his film this weekend. Film industry outlet Variety reported, external that an X message embedded with a high-quality version of the film gathered 2.1 million views in two-and-a-half hours on Saturday, before the account was suspended. "The full odyssey movie in a tweet, as nolan intended," one user joked. Nolan shot the entire three-hour movie on 70mm film, a large, high-resolution format designed for giant Imax screens. "The whole Odyssey film in an embedded video on Twitter. Crazy," wrote someone in a post on X. "Someone leaked The Odyssey movie in HD. I thought it was fake but it's true," said another user. The Hollywood Reporter said, external a lower-quality version appeared on X on Sunday, and was removed two hours later after amassing almost 50,000 views. In response, film studio Universal said: "We became aware of the unauthorised posting of the film and immediately initiated takedown protocols. "We take copyright infringement seriously and will pursue all appropriate remedies to protect our content and intellectual property rights." The leak is unlikely to do significant harm to the film's box office performance - it earned $215m (£160m) around the world in its second weekend, taking its total to $640m (£480m). Related topics - Published4 days ago

item.title: Infantino tells Fifa critics to 'meditate, pray or watch football'
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/sport/football/articles/cz0515973gpo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Infantino tells Fifa critics to 'meditate, pray or watch football' - Published Fifa president Gianni Infantino has told critics to "meditate, pray or watch a football match" instead of "spreading hate and false rumours" about his leadership, the governing body and the World Cup. In a 15-slide post on his personal Instagram account - reposted to Fifa's eight million followers - Infantino addressed "those behind their pens and papers, behind their screens" to affirm his belief that, while they were "busy planting seeds of hate", Fifa was delivering the "greatest event on earth". He said the World Cup "celebrated humanity at its best", adding that the 2026 tournament had "100% safety and security, only joy and happiness". Infantino downplayed several of the tournament's high-profile controversies and hailed the involvement of Iran, who featured at the World Cup despite their ongoing conflict with co-hosts the United States, as a success. He said Fifa "worked tirelessly to unite two countries at war", with Iran entering the country "without incident or conflict". His comments are in stark contradiction to those of Iran's head coach Amir Ghalenoei, who said his team were the "most oppressed" at the World Cup. - Infantino's 'time is up' with Fifa - La Liga boss - Published5 days ago
- The country that doesn't play football... yet - Published6 days ago
Iran faced visa delays, "integral" members of their backroom staff were denied entry to the US and fans had their allocation of tickets revoked, while Iran also had to move their training base from Tucson, Arizona to Tijuana, Mexico following a multitude of logistical issues in the build up to the tournament. They later also encountered restrictions on their movements as they travelled between their training base and group matches in Los Angeles and Seattle. Such issues were not unique to Iran, with fans from Haiti, Senegal, and Ivory Coast impacted by travel bans imposed by the Trump administration, while Somali referee Omar Artan was denied entry to the US - despite holding a diplomatic passport and a single entry US visa - because of his "association with suspected members of terror organisations". Infantino wrote: "You mentioned the few people denied visas and overlooked the millions who were approved, from all parts of the world. Because football unites the world, and it was impressively demonstrated this summer." Doubling down on the tournament's safety, Infantino said there were "zero incidents, zero violence, just joy, emotions, happiness, unity, and togetherness". However, Fifa is investigating Argentina's actions after players and backroom staff were involved in altercations with Spain's players after losing the World Cup final. It is also investigating allegations of racist abuse towards American social media influencer IShowSpeed, while supporters were arrested at multiple matches - including following England's semi-final against Argentina in Atlanta. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officials were also controversially present at World Cup stadiums. Infantino also addressed criticism surrounding the standard of officiating at the tournament, in particular concerns about political interference after USA forward Folarin Balogun was made available for their last-16 tie when his one-match ban was suspended by Fifa - following the intervention of US President Donald Trump. Of the 191 other red cards shown at a men's World Cup, only one other player has escaped a suspension. Uefa said the decision had "crossed a red line", labelling it "unprecedented, incomprehensible, and unjustifiable", while the Norwegian Football Federation is considering filing a formal complaint to Fifa's ethics committee. Infantino, however, argued that such decisions are not out of the ordinary, claiming similar rulings are "routine and widely accepted in some of the biggest leagues worldwide". He added: "It's curious that the same countries employing these practices are the ones criticising." The International Olympic Committee has said it will not investigate Infantino for any possible breaches of political neutrality, stating the complaint levelled by human rights campaign group FairSquare falls outside the jurisdiction of its ethics commission. Infantino's advice to his opponents was "to show some love" and "respect" to a tournament where "people came together as families, as fans, as one". "To everyone who missed our beautiful game, the emotions, the celebrations, the laughter, the crying, the deception and the joy. To all of you who missed watching kids, babies, grandparents and parents come together for the beautiful game... sorry that you were so consumed by hate and criticism that you missed it all," Infantino wrote. "While they celebrated, you were busy planting seeds of hate. Our world needs love, not hate; tolerance, not division; celebration, not mourning. "To those spending their time and energy hating us, please take a moment to reflect, meditate, pray or watch a football match and truly observe the faces, the eyes, the emotions. "Because only our beautiful game can deliver such an extraordinary show, a show where everyone becomes one and reconnects as humans. "I am incredibly proud, as Fifa President, to have contributed, even a little, to this show. It's a great feeling." Related topics - Published11 July
- Published18 July

item.title: Argentinian leader calls Brazilian president a 'thief' and a 'convict'
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cvgx91vdedno?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Argentinian leader calls Brazilian president a 'thief' and a 'convict' - Published Brazil has recalled its ambassador to Buenos Aires after Argentina's president hit out at the Brazilian president, referring to him as a "thief" and a "convict". Javier Milei made the comments on Sunday at a rally in Sao Paulo to launch the presidential campaign of right-wing candidate Flávio Bolsonaro, who is set to run in an election in October. Without naming Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva explicitly, he referred to the Brazilian president derogatorily while speaking alongside Bolsonaro, who he went on to say was the only one who could "stop Lula". Brazilian diplomats later said the Argentine leader had insulted Brazil's government, its people, and its democracy. Speaking later on Sunday, Lula said he would continue to lead "without anyone's interference," and that "in Brazil, we do not accept anyone sticking their nose where it doesn't belong". Brazil's ambassador to Argentina, Julio Bitelli, was due to return home between Sunday and Monday, AFP reported. Flavio Bolsanaro is the son of Brazil's former president, Jair Bolsonaro, who was last year sentenced to more than 27 years in jail for plotting a coup aimed at keeping him in power after he lost the last election to Lula. The judge who oversaw the conviction of Jair Bolsonaro, Brazilian Supreme Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes, was also referred to by Milei as "bald trash". Moraes had also previously denied Milei permission to visit the former president while he was under house arrest in Brasilia. In 2018, Lula was sentenced to 12 years in prison over a massive corruption and bribery scandal, but was released after serving a little over 18 months. Lula's convictions were annulled by the Supreme Court in 2021 and in presidential elections the following year he narrowly beat far-right incumbent Jair Bolsonaro, winning 50.9% of the vote. item.title: Rapper Yung Filly tells trial 'vibes were good' with woman who accuses him of rape
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cm2g044ydl4o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Rapper Yung Filly tells trial 'vibes were good' with woman who accuses him of rape - Published UK rapper Yung Filly has told a court that the "vibes were good" between him and a woman he is accused of raping after performing at a nightclub in Australia in 2024. The rapper, whose real name is Andres Felipe Valencia Barrientos, took the witness stand at the District Court of Western Australia on Monday - a week after the start of his trial. He is accused of sexually assaulting the woman, then 20 years old, in his hotel room after he performed in Hillarys, a coastal suburb of Perth. Barrientos, 30, has pleaded not guilty to six counts of sexual penetration without consent, three counts of assault occasioning bodily harm, and one count of strangulation. Barrientos told the court he had "fancied" the woman when they met at the concert venue. He had been in the VIP area while she leaned over the barrier from the general area. He denied touching her inappropriately. "I recall putting my hand on her waist," he told the court. But he said he had not put his hands down her pants or touched her breast. The "vibes were good" between them later when they arrived at his hotel, Barrientos said. His security guard took the woman's phone away - a "standard practice" to protect their privacy, according to Barrientos. The court heard previously that the pair had engaged in consensual sex before Barrientos turned violent and she told him to stop. Barrientos, who had been touring Australia at the time of the alleged offences, is also known for his work with the YouTube collective Beta Squad, and has appeared in the celebrity version of Bake Off on Channel 4 and presented BBC Three shows. He has been on bail since being charged and was allowed to fly home to the UK in September for four months, before returning to Western Australia ahead of his trial. In addition to his 1.8 million YouTube subscribers, he has three million followers on TikTok and and 2.4 million on Instagram.

item.title: Australian court upholds racial discrimination ruling against Pauline Hanson
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cx2k5v9202wo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Australian court upholds racial discrimination ruling against Pauline Hanson - Published Australian populist leader Pauline Hanson racially discriminated against a Muslim senator in a 2022 tweet by telling her to return to Pakistan, a court has said, upholding an earlier ruling. The One Nation party leader had appealed a 2024 ruling that she had breached the racial discrimination act when she responded to a post by Senator Mehreen Faruqi with an "angry personal attack" that was "anti-Muslim". Hanson had argued at the Federal Court that political communication should be protected but Justice Melissa Perry dismissed her appeal on Monday. "Today's win is for every single person who has been made to feel that their belonging in this country is conditional," Faruqi said outside court. "This case was always about holding to account racism and holding to account those who perpetrate racism," she added. "Hate speech is not free speech." On the day of the death of Queen Elizabeth II in September 2022, Faruqi had offered condolences to those who mourned for the queen in a social media post. But, she added, "I cannot mourn the leader of a racist empire built on stolen lives, land and wealth of colonized people." Hanson responded with a post that was "a variant of the slogan, 'go back to where you came from'", Judge Angus Stewart ruled in 2024. The phrase was "a racist trope with a long history", and "implicitly" targeted Muslims, he said. He ordered Hanson to delete the tweet and pay Faruqi's legal costs. Faruqi, the deputy leader of the Greens party, took Hanson to court after the tweet was posted, arguing it breached the racial discrimination act. It was reasonably likely to offend, insult, humiliate or intimidate another person or group of people and was done because of her race, colour or national or ethnic origin, she argued. Hanson said she was "disappointed" with the decision and that she and her legal team would review it "with a view to commencing an appeal in the High Court of Australia". Hanson has in the past advocated for a "Muslim ban" on immigration and earlier this year attracted criticism for an interview in which she suggested there were no "good" Muslims. This month Hanson denied that she was advocating for a return of the "White Australia" policy - when from 1901 to the 1970s the nation banned non-white immigrants - in a podcast with British far-right activist Tommy Robinson. In the podcast, Robinson asked Hanson how Australia had ended up with "Pakistanis, Somalis, all of these African problems with violent Africans?" to which Hanson responded that it began when "they opened up and got rid of the White Australian policy".

item.title: Shein swings to $99m loss as Trump tariffs hit sales
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/clyj8v0rek8o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Shein swings to $99m loss as Trump tariffs hit sales - Published Shein says it swung to a quarterly loss as its sales slowed after US President Donald Trump removed an import duty exemption on small packages. It also comes as uncertainty remains over the tit-for-tat US-China tariffs wars, which is currently paused. The fast-fashion giant, which has its headquarters in Singapore but was founded in China, said it lost $99m (£74.1m) in the first three months of the year, compared with a net income of $395m a year earlier. The announcement is part of the firm's preparations ahead of its stock market debut in Hong Kong, although the filing did not give any details on the size, timetable or pricing of the planned initial public offering (IPO). "In response to the increased duties and taxes, we are pursuing a wide range of options, including increasing our prices in the US market to offset a portion of the increased costs," Shein said in the filing. The company also said the Iran war had hit demand, increased costs and caused delays of deliveries in some markets. The first-quarter figures also partly reflected a paper loss of $328m due to an accounting change for special investor shares. The shares can be turned into ordinary stock later, and their value can change before a listing. The filing showed that in the year to the end of March 2026 Shein had 281 million active customers - a rise of more than 16% on a year earlier - who placed a total of more than one billion orders. On 10 July, the China Securities Regulatory Commission (CSRC) gave Shein approval for a Hong Kong share sale after failed attempts to list in New York and London. The Hong Kong share listing is expected to take place in the coming months. The figures show the impact of a Trump-signed executive order to end a global tariff exemption that had been used by US shoppers of low-cost goods. That order, which came into effect on 29 August 2025, broadened an earlier presidential action which specifically targeted cheap products from China and Hong Kong to cover the rest of the world. The so-called de minimis exemption had allowed goods valued at $800 or less to enter the US without paying any tariffs. US consumers relied on the exemption to buy cheap goods from online commerce sites like Shein and Temu. The White House said the global exemption was being used to "evade tariffs and funnel deadly synthetic opioids" to the US. "The removal of the US de minimis exemption has had an adverse impact on our sales in the US and the overall growth of our net revenues," Shein said in the filing. Earlier in July, the European Union imposed a €3 (£2.56; $3.42) levy on low-value e-commerce imports. The measure is aimed to curb what the trading bloc has said is unfair competition from China.

item.title: Chinese chipmaker shares surge 470% in blockbuster stock market debut
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c9q9w3x9qn2o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Chinese chipmaker shares surge 470% in blockbuster stock market debut - Published Shares in China's biggest memory chip maker have surged by more than 470% as they made their debut on the Shanghai Stock Exchange's tech-heavy Star Market. The surge has pushed ChangXin Memory Technologies' (CXMT) stock market valuation to around 3.3 trillion yuan ($487.3bn; £364.9bn), making it the most valuable listed company in mainland China. The spectacular debut comes despite a sharp sell-off in technology stocks around the world this month. CXMT manufactures dynamic random-access memory (Dram) chips that power artificial intelligence (AI) data centres, mobile phones, PCs, tablets and other devices. The firm, which was founded in 2016 by Chairman Zhu Yiming, is headquartered in Hefei, Anhui Province in eastern China. The company has said it plans to use most of the proceeds from the initial public offering (IPO) to boost production of memory chips and carry out more research and developments. The stellar performance of its IPO will offer some comfort to Chinese financial officials, who have been rolling out measures to help curb a stock market slump that wiped out more than $1.5tn in recent weeks. Analysts said the jump was also being driven by demand for the shares far outstripping supply. "The reason for the extraordinary bounce this morning is that only 7% of the shares are available for trading," Anna Macdonald, investment strategy director at Hargreaves Lansdown told the BBC's Today programme. It also highlights Chinese investors' strong appetite for a homegrown chipmaker, as the government in Beijing pushes ahead with plans to make its technology industry self-reliant. South Korean tech giants Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix and US-based Micron dominate the Dram market, with the three companies accounting for around 90% of global production. Earlier this month, SK Hynix raised $26.5bn (£19.8bn) in its New York share offering, marking the largest ever listing by a foreign firm in the US. The company, a key supplier to AI chip giant Nvidia, said it had sold 177.9 million American depositary shares for $149 each. The shares surged as much as 17% on Friday in their first day of trading on the Nasdaq but have since given up some of that gain. SK Hynix saw its market value top $1tn in its home country in May, lifted by the boom in demand for AI chips.

item.title: 'This is just the start': India's Gen Z protesters force out a minister, but what next?
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c8dng1v72lno?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
'This is just the start': India's Gen Z protesters force out a minister, but what next? - Published In 12 years of Narendra Modi's rule in India , only one cabinet minister had previously resigned - over allegations of sexual misconduct. So education minister Dharmendra Pradhan's resignation on Saturday, after more than a week of intense street protests, became a defining moment - one many young people celebrated as a rare victory. In the words of 22-year-old Sakhi, a student activist in Delhi, "for the first time, it felt like we can make things happen through protests". Soon after Pradhan quit, social media seized on an old video of a senior Modi minister boasting that "resignations do not happen in our government", reflecting the confidence of the nationwide youth movement that had demanded his exit. Sakhi says they grew up reading textbooks that spoke about the importance of dissent in a democracy, "but I did not see that around me in the Modi years". On Instagram, Sakhi posted photos and videos of police assaults and detentions alongside reels mocking officers standing beside them. Many have been viewed millions of times. Sakhi says the government failed to grasp the movement's momentum because it was out of touch with the language and platforms of the protests. "The government has a hold on mainstream media, Facebook and WhatsApp. But it missed Instagram." The latest education protests erupted in May after NEET, India's biggest medical entrance exam, was cancelled following a question paper leak, forcing nearly two million students to retake the test. More than 20 students died by suicide, with their families blaming the scandal. The outrage was channelled by the satirical Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), an online campaign launched after India's chief justice likened unemployed people with "fake and bogus degrees" to cockroaches. Its founders staged a sit-in in Delhi, demanding Pradhan's resignation, education reforms and compensation for the bereaved families. Initially, the protest drew little attention. That changed on 18 July when Delhi police forcibly removed and hospitalised hunger-striking educator Sonam Wangchuk. Two days later, tens of thousands marched on parliament at the CJP's call, triggering a police crackdown. Videos of baton charges, tear gas and pellet guns spread rapidly online, fuelling public anger and swelling the protests instead of suppressing them. The discontent among India's youth and the courage to voice it on the streets spread to other parts of the country. Somaya Korde was detained at home after urging people online to join a 20 July protest in Mumbai, but went on to attend multiple demonstrations in the days that followed. Pradhan's resignation, says the 26-year-old, "is not the end, but just the beginning". "For this generation, this is the first time many of us have stepped out to protest. But there are larger issues to talk about, and we will talk about them," she says. Korde, the first woman in her family to graduate in law and a recent civic election candidate, comes from a community officially classified as "backward" because of its historic social and economic disadvantage. Like many young Indians, she saw education as her path to a better life, but says the NEET paper leak shattered her faith in a system that promised hard work would be rewarded. "Schools and colleges are being privatised, paper leaks are happening, even if you finish education, there are not enough jobs. In a democracy, all this raises questions of accountability against the government," she says. Her frustration is indicative of a larger picture. India has the world's largest youth population, yet unemployment among 15- to 29-year-olds rose to 16.2% in June from 13.8% a year earlier, according to government data. Even graduates are struggling: a 2026 Azim Premji University study found fewer than 7% of jobseekers secured permanent salaried work within a year, and fewer than 4% landed white-collar jobs. The protests became a rallying point for young people to shed their caution and voice their frustration. Among them was 18-year-old Harshvardhan Kadam, who took a part-time job selling laptops after finishing school to help support his mother following his father's death last year. On 23 July, a video Harshvardhan filmed during a protest march in Mumbai went viral. In the Instagram reel, now viewed 10 million times, a policeman is seen threatening to frame him in a fake drugs case while detaining him in a police van. The constable has since been suspended. "I did not wish him to be suspended," Kadam told the BBC, "I just wanted to document how the police were treating me for participating in a peaceful protest." Now, reflecting on Pradhan's resignation he says: "This is just the start. This shows that next time the government will be scared when we raise our voices." Swaraj Priyo, a 29-year-old screenwriter from Guwahati, says years of protesting under the Modi government had left him disillusioned by the lack of change. But this movement, he says, has restored hope: "This movement has brought back space for question and dissent and the reality check that all is not over." A growing sense that the Modi government is on the back foot is palpable. Protest sites across the country now display posters declaring: "Pradhan was just an example. It's Modi's turn next". But alongside this bullishness comes some apprehension. Varuni Poorva, a 30-year-old aspiring professor from Patna and a student activist for nearly a decade, says Pradhan's resignation shows the Modi government can be "brought to its knees". But she fears a "witch hunt" against protesters despite the government's pledge not to act against those who organised or joined the demonstrations. Over the past week, she has sought anticipatory bail to guard against possible arrest. Police have charged more than 100 protesters with offences including attempted murder, and arrested more than 40. Human Rights Watch says, external that under Modi, Indian authorities have "routinely prosecuted activists, journalists, and peaceful protesters on fabricated counterterrorism and hate speech laws". Despite fears of a crackdown, shared by many students' parents, Poorva believes the protests have given young people newfound confidence. With their deeper frustrations unresolved, she says, it will be difficult for the government to return to "business as usual". At one protest site in Delhi, graffiti captures the mood: "We do not have jobs. If you wipe this out, we will come back tomorrow".

item.title: What we know so far about the Berlin Pride ramming attack
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cevmdxz4872o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
What we know so far about the Berlin Pride ramming attack - Published One woman has been killed and at least 29 others injured after a van was driven into a crowd at a Berlin Pride event on Saturday night, in what officials say was likely an "Islamist terror attack". The suspect, 21-year-old Abdul Ballout, has been shot and killed during a police operation in west Berlin. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has condemned the incident as a "heinous" attack. Here is what we know so far. What happened in the Berlin Pride attack? The attack happened at about 22:00 local time (20:00 GMT). A report was made to police in Berlin that a white vehicle had been driven into crowds at a Pride event in the capital. Hundreds of thousands of people had gathered at Tiergarten park, near the iconic Brandenburg Gate, for the annual event, which is known as Christopher Street Day. Some people were also stabbed in the incident, with a blade officials believe could have been a machete. Shortly afterwards, the Pride event was cancelled. A performance was abruptly brought to a end, with organisers taking to the stage and advising the crowd to start walking towards the exits. As the message was being given to the crowd, the word "evacuation" was projected onto a large screen on the stage. Unverified video posted to social media showed large crowds of people leaving the scene as emergency vehicles raced to the scene. At about 01:00 local time, police confirmed that one woman had been killed and many more had suffered injuries. A short time later, police confirmed they had found the vehicle believed to have been used in the attack, saying it had crashed into a tree. The vehicle is believed to have been rented. At about 03:30, police said on X they had identified a suspect with Islamist links. The search area was widened to the entire city and involved thousands of police, including officers from surrounding German states. On Sunday, police officers stood guard outside an apartment block in Berlin's Tiergarten district, which is said to be the suspect's home. Police say he was later shot and killed at an allotment complex in Spandau, a borough in the west of the capital, after he rushed at officers with a knife. Who is the suspect in the Berlin Pride attack? The suspect has been named by police as 21-year-old Abdul Ballout, a German citizen of Lebanese background. He was known to police and had been radicalised, officials said. A statement released by the Berlin public prosecutor's office revealed further details about Ballout's criminal history. In May 2025, prosecutors said he travelled via Turkey to Lebanon, with the intention of joining the Islamic State group (IS) in Syria. While in Lebanon he allegedly made contact with several individuals he believed were members of IS. He was arrested in Lebanon in July 2025 and sentenced to three months in prison for incitement to religious and sectarian conflict. Then in November 2025 he returned to Germany where he was arrested at Berlin Brandenburg Airport and held in pre-trial detention. In May this year, he was sentenced to one year and 10 months in prison for "preparing a serious act of violence endangering the state". The decision was deferred for six months and he was placed under the supervision of a parole officer. He was previously convicted of assault and robbery in 2022, and of robbing a victim of headphones in 2020. Where did the attack happen? The attack took place in the popular Tiergarten park, near the Brandenberg Gate. A large number of people and floats took part in the Christopher Street Day event, which passed through the city, before moving through Tiergarten park, past the Victory Column monument, and towards the Brandenberg Gate. Berlin Police have said people were hit on Ahornsteig, which is a long path stretching across the park, largely in a forested area. European leaders have been swift to condemn the attack. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen expressed her sympathy to the victims, saying the Pride event stands for "freedom, dignity, and equality - the fundamental values of the EU". "Every person should be able to live, love, and stand up for their rights without fear," she wrote on social media. Rob Jetten, prime minister of the Netherlands, said the Dutch stand "shoulder to shoulder with our German neighbours", while Italy's prime minister Georgia Meloni expressed "solidarity and sincere sympathy". The UK's defence secretary Wes Streeting called the incident "an absolutely horrific disaster", adding his thoughts and prayers are with the German people. Did you attend Berlin Pride? item.title: The notorious Cameroonian prison with its own record label
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/czxqlkrlj7no?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
The notorious Cameroonian prison with its own record label - Published New Bell - a notorious prison in Douala, Cameroon - is a city within a city. The facility has its own "taxis" (inmates who whizz through congested courtyards on foot to hand deliver messages), its own law enforcement (burly prisoners who help stretched guards police the facility) and market (a string of stalls where convicts sell and buy goodies, like fried cassava and beignet pastries). Basically, the occupants of New Bell have adapted the jail's slack laws to work for them. The clearest example of this spirit is Jail Time Records, an on-site music studio and label making mini stars out of the most talented prisoners. Empereur, the feared leader of gangs inside and outside of the prison, has amassed 24,000 YouTube views with a music video filmed entirely in prison. Songs from the inmates have gained fans from as far away as South Africa, the US and Argentina, while earlier this year Jail Time Records put on a huge concert for the prisoners in New Bell's courtyard. "It's this instrument of resistance… where we can really share friendship, love and our voices can be heard," Steve Happi, the former inmate who co-founded Jail Time Records, tells the BBC's Talking Movies programme. "We don't think anymore about the four walls - we find the freedom." The Jail Time Records studio is rudimentary - a small, sweaty recording booth attached to a room inhabited by a solitary computer. But it is also the site of great catharsis and creativity, as per a recent, acclaimed documentary named after the studio. Directed by Happi and Italian artist Dione Roach, his Jail Time Records co-founder, it was filmed in New Bell over six years. Last month it won three prizes, including best documentary feature, at New York's Tribeca film festival. In the film, a prisoner named Stone raps into the studio's microphone: "Heart of stone, it's war. My senses shatter like broken glass. "I'm closed and tight like a cell door. No solid ground I slip like a fish." Stone, who used to be a soldier in Cameroon's presidential guard, was sentenced to 10 years in New Bell for robbery and illegal possession of firearms. He insists he is not guilty. The film captures him trying - often unsuccessfully - to reach his young daughter Maira on the phone. "It's been a long time. She needs to hear my voice from time to time, so she doesn't forget about her father," he says in a voice message to a family member, after failing to get through to Maira yet again. The music video for Heart of Stone is a typical Jail Time Records affair. The production value is high, storytelling is captivating and hordes of fellow inmates get involved as actors and crew. "The music that comes out of there is amazing," says Taika Waititi, the New Zealand Oscar-winning director who, with his wife, the singer Rita Ora, served as an executive producer for the Jail Time Records documentary. "Just in terms of the power of art in relation to redemption and what that can mean to someone who, you know, some of these people are in prison for life. I think having an outlet is an incredibly powerful and humane thing," he says. Jail Time Records was founded in 2018, when Roach volunteered for a non-profit organisation running events inside New Bell. During a dance class for the prisoners, a crew of rappers took over the microphone and began freestyling. Impressed by their performance, she asked the prison authorities for permission to start up a studio. The powers that be were receptive and so Roach enlisted Happi to run the studio as a producer and sound engineer. According to Happi, he ended up in New Bell following a family argument over what should be done with his late father's body. Amid the dispute, his aunt, a high court judge, allegedly arranged for him to be thrown into jail for killing his father. He was acquitted of the crime two years later, Jail Time Records says. In 2022, Happi, Roach and the prisoners released an album named Jail Time Vol 1. As is customary for Jail Time Records' music, half the profit from the album's sale went to the artists and the rest was reinvested into the label. The studio's survival is paramount to many of the artists, especially given New Bell's bitter environment. In 2022, Human Rights Watch reported that New Bell was housing 4,700 prisoners within its crumbling walls - four times its capacity. The prison's packed population, along with its unsanitary conditions, enabled cholera to spread rapidly during an outbreak four years ago, rights groups have said. At least six inmates died from the disease. New Bell also has a reputation for violence. In 2008, guards shot 16 inmates dead during an attempted breakout. Prisoners also attack and intimidate each other - the documentary captures Empereur, who is serving 10 years for multiple crimes, shaking down a bewildered young inmate for a necklace chain and some flip-flops. Asked if the Jail Time Records project might glorify Empereur, the son of a traditional Douala chief, and other criminals who have committed violent crimes, Roach tells the BBC: "The process we're doing is a rehabilitation process, basically. "We enter the prison without any judgment and it's the only way we can really approach this kind of work. "Music, as with any creative process, is also a way of self-discovery... coming to terms with things you've done and hopefully changing for the better". The prison authorities appear to share this view. "They were really welcoming of the project. Cameroon is a super musical country… everyone loves music," Happi says, adding that the head of the prison attended this year's concert and proceeded to dance with the performers. With official support, Jail Time Records has been able to flourish, offering opportunities to more prisoners, including those in New Bell's women's wing. Jeje, Jail Time Records first female artist, made her debut in 2022 with brooding Afrobeats song Show Me The Way. "Nobody show me the way, nobody show me the way, I did it all alone," sings Jeje, who was jailed after stealing money and running away from an allegedly abusive uncle. As well as working with the women's wing, Jail Time Records have expanded their project outside New Bell and Cameroon. Roach and Happi set up a studio 1,000 miles (1,600km) away in 2023, in the central prison of Burkina Faso's capital city, Ouagadougou. Jail Time Records hopes it can replicate the success of the original New Bell studio, with its accompanying label, music video production arm and now, award-winning documentary. The film ends with an "in memoriam" sequence; a tribute to six prisoners who died while the Jail Time Records project has been running. New Bell may appear to be endlessly bleak, but according to Happi, music provides the inmates with a "lantern for a brighter future". "Before that, they had the stubborn mentality: it's them against the world," he says. "They feel now important - they feel like they have a place in the society." item.title: Left-wing Democrats are on a winning run - but can they lure back crucial swing voters?
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c5y3rrd32jlo?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Left-wing Democrats are on a winning run - but can they lure back crucial swing voters? - Published On a Saturday evening in Michigan, the skies still hazy from drifting Canadian wildfire smoke, hundreds of voters packed into Detroit's opulent 104-year-old Opera House, rising from their seats to cheer loudly as Senator Bernie Sanders and Democratic Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez took the stage. As two of the leading figures on the American left, Ocasio-Cortez and Sanders were there to champion Senate hopeful Abdul El-Sayed - a doctor running on a platform of universal healthcare. His supporters carried signs with El-Sayed's slogan "Medicare for All", and wore shirts urging the end of immigration enforcement and US aid to Israel. But they were not the only ones tuning in. Voters and politicians across the country are watching to see if El-Sayed can earn the Democratic nomination to run for Senate in November's midterm elections. His opponent - Congresswoman Haley Stevens - is an experienced politician with deep pockets, thanks in part to large corporate campaign donations. The two represent the divisions within the Democratic Party as it seeks to take back control of Congress. On one side is the centrist establishment, backed by traditional power players. On the other is the left wing of the party, exemplified by Sanders and Ocasio-Cortez as well as New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani. But while left-wing Democrats have seen a wave of victories during this summer's primaries - including in New York and Colorado - what remains to be seen is if they can claw back support from disillusioned working-class voters, who flocked to President Donald Trump in 2024. In Michigan - which voted for Democrat Joe Biden in 2020 but Trump four years later - the open Senate seat is a must-win for Democrats. The seat had been held by one of their own, and if the party hopes to make gains in the Senate, and halt Trump's agenda, they will need to keep a hold of it. Whoever wins the primary on 4 August will be competing against Trump ally Mike Rogers come 3 November. At Saturday's rally, some in the crowd felt hopeful, as Ocasio-Cortez promised El-Sayed represented the "politics of the future". But miles outside the venue, other voters were less certain of his ability to beat Stevens - or to secure a victory for the Democrats by touting policies like healthcare for all and staunch opposition to Israel's military campaign in Gaza. "This may not be the moment for progressives," said Colleen Houlihan, a 74-year-old from Ferndale, Michigan who is likely voting for Stevens. "I want radical change in the country, but we've got to start with this administration and it's got to be an electable candidate to get power back in sane hands." El-Sayed is locked in a tight race against Stevens, a moderate Democrat who has pitched herself as the more experienced congresswoman and earned the endorsement of Michigan's governor Gretchen Whitmer as well as outgoing Senator Gary Peters. It is not the only test of progressive power in a midwestern battleground state, as self-described Democratic socialist Francesca Hong attempts to secure a win in the governor's race in neighbouring Wisconsin just a week later. Some political experts and voters questioned whether the current momentum would be enough to win over voters in the politically diverse, and historically working-class, midwest. "They got a big win electing Mamdani mayor of New York City, but also, it's New York City," said Adrian Hemond, a political strategist in Michigan. "They have been much less able to win in some more traditionally purple areas." 'Medicare for All' and affordability take centre stage On a humid morning before Saturday's rally, Corie Johnson was knocking on voters' doors for the first time in her life. The 35-year-old has always voted for Democrats, but said El-Sayed is the first candidate she has felt excited about. "We're not so stuck in our ways," she said of millennial voters. "I think that's why he's gaining so much momentum." Walking by the rowhouses on the streets of Hamtramck, a small town within Detroit, Johnson and her fellow canvassers were attempting to carry on a pitch they had heard from El-Sayed in a meeting just moments before. "Money out of politics, money in pockets, Medicare for all," El-Sayed and his group of volunteers chanted together in the campaign's Detroit office. The former Wayne County health director's policy plans - including universal healthcare and an annual wealth tax on billionaires - represent a pivot for a Democratic Party that has seen one of its lowest favourability ratings in recent years. In 2025, the number of Democrats who viewed their own party positively fell by 12% to 67%, according to a Gallup poll, external. Despite his left-wing stances, El-Sayed has avoided the label claimed by many of his peers: Democratic socialist. But he is still taking lessons from their wins, especially Mamdani, whose social media skills and laser focus on affordability helped propel him to victory in New York. El-Sayed's affordability platform - including his focus on health insurance - is why Les Lukacs of Monroe, Michigan, is voting for him. The longstanding Democrat who does not have health insurance said he would not vote for Stevens in November if El-Sayed lost the primary. "We can barely afford groceries and gas," he said. "I have to make sacrifices - and healthcare is one of them." Polling from the last year suggests healthcare costs remain among the top issues for voters in the November midterms, alongside the rising cost of gas, groceries and housing. El-Sayed told the BBC that if the Democratic Party had more concerns for everyday people, "they'd be fighting on the same policies I'm fighting for". In a statement to the BBC, a spokesperson for Stevens' campaign said the congresswoman would "fight for all Michiganders from every zip code to lower costs, protect manufacturing jobs, and take on Donald Trump's corruption and abuses of power". Israel a key test for Democratic candidates Following in the footsteps of his peers on the left of his party, El-Sayed has spoken out against US involvement in the Middle East, including aid to Israel. Recent polling suggests a growing portion of voters believe the US is too supportive of its longtime ally in the wake of the war. The issue has particular resonance in Michigan, which is home to the second largest Arab-American population in the US. El-Sayed - the son of Egyptian immigrants - has called Israel's actions in Gaza a genocide. He has also been quick to invoke his opponent's ties to AIPAC (the American Israel Public Affairs Committee), which has spent almost $30m to back Stevens in the race. Like many more moderate Democrats, Stevens has said she supports upholding US aid to Israel without conditions. She did not respond to a request for comment from the BBC on her stance on Israel. Rex Nazarko, the leader of the American Muslim Engagement and Empowerment Network, believes El-Sayed will pick up some of the thousands of Democrats in the state who chose not to support Kamala Harris and Joe Biden in the 2024 presidential election because of their stance on Israel. Cedric Erkins, a sheriff's deputy in Auburn Hills, Michigan, who has not decided his vote, is frustrated by costs skyrocketing in the US, while the country "can afford to send billions overseas". While the Democratic Party has been mostly united against Trump's war in Iran, the Israel-Gaza war continues to present a dilemma for Democrats, who have historically depended on votes from both the Jewish and Arab communities to win elections, said Larry Sabato, the director of the University of Virginia Center for Politics "They have to make a choice," he said. "Both sides are trying to make it as painful as possible." Sewing a 'frayed' Democratic Party back together As some left-wing voters rally behind El-Sayed, other Democrats remain worried about whether the movement is popular enough to help Democrats win back swing states. Sally, a 45-year-old Michigan resident who declined to share her last name because she is an elected official, said she was excited by the movement's enthusiasm, but wasn't sure it was sustainable. "There's a lot of that momentum, but keeping that momentum going is really hard," she said. She added that even though Stevens had been attacked for her ties to corporate campaign funding, big money helps in politics. "It's those connections that are going to support changes in law and make things move faster," she said. Some of El-Sayed's voters, steadfast in their support, also worried whether their votes would be enough. "I'm a little scared. I'm a little nervous," said Claire McHugh, a 70-year-old who went to the rally. "I just hope that enough people are fed up with the status quo." Asked whether he believed left-wing candidates could win over more moderate Democrats to beat Republicans, El-Sayed told the BBC that he was not concerned with the future of the Democratic Party. But, he added, "If Democrats want to find their future, I think we're showing it to them right here." Sabato said it remained to be seen which faction of the Democratic Party would prevail. But regardless, he said, Democrats would have to find a way to "sew these two very large groups back together" if they wanted to reverse recent election losses. "It's already frayed," he said. "If they don't do the repair job they need to do and quickly, certainly through 2028, then they're going to have to get used to losing." - Published30 June

item.title: The woman promoting the UK pottery region to Japan
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cy7405m8ke1o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
The woman promoting the Potteries to Japan - Published A woman has been praised for her efforts in promoting the city of Stoke-on-Trent to Japan. Yuri Kawakami-Shotton runs Peak and Pottery Tours at the city's Spode Museum, showcasing the region and the Potteries to overseas visitors from Japan. She said she was inspired to spread the word about the city after watching a BBC News report about pottery firms falling into administration. "My father-in-law said: 'Oh, because no one's buying a dinner set anymore'," she explained. "And I said, 'Japanese people would buy, Japanese people would go to the museum and things. I can do that, I can maybe promote it for this city'." Kawakami-Shotton said, since starting her tours, the dinner sets made in England have proved to be a hit in Japan. "My customers love it and then some of them, for example, they come in Spode, they can't move, in front of the entrance, like 'oh my god i'm in Stoke, i'm in Spode'," she beamed. "It's like a legend." Michael Escolme, manager of the Spode Museum, praised Kawakami-Shotton's efforts to broaden their reach. "She's been a valued member of our team really, ever since bringing Japanese visitors to us both in real life and virtually to the museum," he said. Kawakami-Shotton also brings her visitors to The Rabbit Hole Tea Room in the city. In 2023, she helped the firm take their afternoon tea to Japan, where one part of the menu proved to be very popular. "We were given the amazing opportunity to go and work out at Nihonbashi in Japan where we had a pop-up of The Rabbit Hole in September," said Lee Greenhalgh, the cafe's owner. "That was insane - we went from selling a few hundred scones a day to 2,000 scones a day!" item.title: The Indian Army's first woman boxer is now chasing Commonwealth gold
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c5y0m8z6de3o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
The Indian Army's first woman boxer is now chasing Commonwealth gold - Published The reigning 57kg world champion boxer Jaismine Lamboria from India throws punches for a living, but when it comes to handling pressure, she looks to one of her country's most celebrated cricketing legends for inspiration. "I really admire MS Dhoni's mindset," says the soft-spoken Lamboria of the former Indian captain. "He is known as 'Captain Cool' for a reason, and I want to be calm like him." That composure will be particularly valuable for Lamboria over the coming days. The 24-year-old is one of India's strongest boxing gold-medal prospects at the Glasgow Commonwealth Games, looking to improve on the bronze she won at Birmingham 2022. Coming off a breakout 2025 during which she won World Cup golds in Astana and Delhi before becoming world champion in Liverpool, Lamboria is in Glasgow with an uncomplicated ambition. "I aim to change the colour of that medal to gold," she says. "That's what I've been training and preparing towards." At 5ft 8½in, Lamboria is tall by Indian boxing standards. Her Olympic debut in Paris ended in a first-round defeat to Tokyo silver medallist Nesthy Petecio of the Philippines. But the setback came in the weight class she had only recently returned to. After spending nearly three years boxing at 60kg, Lamboria dropped back to 57kg during the Paris qualification campaign - a move that ultimately paid off when she won the world title by defeating Paris Olympic silver medallist Julia Atena Szeremeta of Poland. "That Paris 2024 Olympics exit was disappointing but it was an eye-opener," says Lamboria. "It prompted several changes in me - physically and mentally. And a significant part of it has come about at the Army Sports Institute (ASI) in Pune, which is where I train." Lamboria credits her ASI coaches for improving his physical strength and a motivational coach and sports psychologist for sharpening her mental game. The Indian Army, however, has provided the wider institutional framework around much of her development. After winning bronze at the 2022 Commonwealth Games, Lamboria became the first female boxer inducted into the army, joining the Corps of Military Police. She now trains under its Mission Olympics Wing. "It's a great honour they wanted to begin with me, but I also see it as an opportunity to become a role model for female athletes," says Lamboria of joining a system that has produced Olympians and Paralympians, including Olympic javelin champion Neeraj Chopra. In early 2024, the Indian Army launched the Girls Sports Company to train girls aged 12 to 16 in four Olympic sports, including boxing, creating a pathway to elite competition and army recruitment. "These girl athletes are doing very well too," says Lamboria. "One boxer has already won Asian Championships gold, which makes me really happy. I may have been the first female boxer in the Indian Army, but I won't be the last." Lamboria's relationship with boxing, however, began long before the army entered her story. Born in the northern state of Haryana, she grew up in Bhiwani, a city synonymous with Indian boxing and widely nicknamed the country's 'Mini Cuba'. Her great-grandfather Hawa Singh was one of Indian boxing's early giants. A heavyweight, he won successive Asian Games gold medals in 1966 and 1970 and was among those who established the famed Bhiwani Boxing Club, which would later produce boxers including Olympic medallist Vijender Singh. Even so, it is not Hawa's medals that feature most prominently in the stories Lamboria remembers hearing about him at home. "He was powerful, but there was also so much humility in him," she says. Her earliest boxing influences were her uncles, Sandeep Singh and Parvinder Singh. "I grew up watching them compete," she says. "They were the ones who got me started." Lamboria began boxing seriously around the age of 14, training first at an academy run by Hawa's son, Sanjay Sheoran, before continuing under her uncles. Though the sport ran through her extended family, Lamboria grew up in a household of modest means. Her father, Jaiveer, works as a home guard, while her mother, Joginder, is a homemaker. "Their support has been a big reason why I was the first girl in my immediate family to take up sport seriously," she says, "not least as the youngest among the girls in the family." Her inspirations, meanwhile, extend well beyond her own family. Lamboria grew up idolising Olympic medallists MC Mary Kom and Vijender Singh. Later, she looked up to Indian Army boxers Amit Panghal and Manish Kaushik, Olympic champion Neeraj Chopra, American swimming great Michael Phelps and Indian sprinting legend Milkha Singh. Closer to home, she credits senior Indian boxers Nikhat Zareen, Lovlina Borgohain and Pooja Rani, not just for their medals but for the encouragement they offer younger athletes. "When you look at them, you naturally feel that you want to do what they have done," she says. Now, Lamboria is beginning to occupy that role herself. "For a long time, boxing has been seen as a male-dominated sport," she says. "Being a woman boxer and an Army athlete, it means a lot to compete on the world stage, prove myself and inspire others through my performances." That change is reflected in the Commonwealth Games too. Boxing has been part of the event since 1930, but women's competition was introduced only in 2014. In Glasgow, bouts began on 24 July, with the finals on 31 July and 1 August. After winning bronze in Birmingham four years ago, Lamboria hopes to leave Glasgow with gold. "When you're competing overseas and the national anthem plays, it's a completely different feeling," she says. "I experienced that at the World Championships in Liverpool last year. That's the moment I want to recreate here."

item.title: Watch: Scaffolding tumbles from Hong Kong building as Typhoon Noul makes landfall
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/videos/ckg9ewekpk1o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Watch: Scaffolding tumbles from Hong Kong building as Typhoon Noul makes landfall Police said they received numerous calls after multi-storey scaffolding along Cheung Sha Wan Road collapsed in powerful winds on Saturday. No injuries have been reported. Typhoon Noul made landfall in southern China on Sunday morning, lashing the region with strong winds and heavy rain and forcing Hong Kong airport to cancel around 360 passenger flights. The typhoon is the strongest to make landfall in China in 2026 to date, according to state media. item.title: Protesters celebrate resignation of India's education minister
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/videos/cly949k3g1do?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
Watch: Protesters celebrate resignation of India's education minister Protesters in India are celebrating after the resignation of the country's education minister, Dharmendra Pradhan. Tens of thousands of young people had been demonstrating in Delhi, demanding Pradhan resign after exam paper leaks and testing irregularities. Now Pradhan has resigned, the protests organised by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) have been called off. CJP is a national movement born out of a satirical campaign, rather than an actual party, and has faced heavy police crackdowns. item.title: India cockroach protests: Videos show officers firing 'pellet guns'
item.description:
【原文链接】：https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/videos/cgje5l292g2o?at_medium=RSS&at_campaign=rss
========================================
India cockroach protests: Videos show officers firing 'pellet guns' Thousands of people have taken to the streets in the Indian capital Delhi as part of the cockroach protests, calling for educational reforms and the resignation of a government minister. BBC Verify has been analysing videos from across the capital, which show security officers firing so-called pellet guns towards protesters. The Central Reserve Police Force didn't respond to our questions about the use of pellet guns and the injuries protesters appeared to sustain. It told media in India it was premature to comment and it was looking into events. Merlyn Thomas and Shruti Menon reports. Produced by Sophie Bott. Graphics by Sally Nicholls.
